description:
We're an international, interdisciplinary team participating in Florianópolis! Our backgrounds combine engineering, computer science, entrepreneurship and tech. We're excited to build a creative, engaging experience for NASA Space Apps 2026.

Main communication language is English. We're looking for teammates with experience or interest in game design, software development, web design, coding, AI and other. All skill levels are welcome - motivation to build matters most
summary:
We built Fire Occurrence Grid Observations (FOGO), a public website that shows when and where Brazil burns, using NASA FIRMS data from 2003 to today.
The challenge asks how to combine MODIS and VIIRS fire detections into one record. They can’t simply be joined: VIIRS has a sharper sensor and picks up several times more fires, so a long-term chart shows a jump that never happened on the ground. We count both satellites in the same unit, days with fire on a roughly 1 km grid, and scale the older MODIS Terra record to match VIIRS NOAA-20, using monthly factors learned from the years when both were in orbit. Tested on 2018–2019, years the method had not seen, it was off by 10% in a typical month.
On the website anyone can choose an area and see its burning calendar, a grid of years and months, plus how unusual each month is, a hotspot map, and files to download. A machine-learning model adds an experimental estimate of fire chance for the coming week.
Researchers get one clean record to work with. Farmers, residents and local authorities get a simple way to understand fire where they live.
details:
NASA has tracked fires from space for over two decades, but with different instruments: MODIS at 1 km since 2000 and VIIRS at 375 m since 2012. VIIRS sees far more small fires, so on one chart it looks as if fire activity in Brazil suddenly jumped, when really only the sensor changed.

Fire Occurrence Grid Observations fixes that. We turned NASA FIRMS hotspots from MODIS Terra and VIIRS NOAA-20 into one consistent record for Brazil from 2003 to today. We count "fire-days" on a roughly 1 km grid and convert the older MODIS record into its VIIRS equivalent, using monthly correction factors learned from the years when both satellites were flying. Tested on years the method had never seen, the median error was 10 %.

The result is a public website built around a burning calendar: a years × months grid showing when and how strongly any region burns, with comparisons against the long-term average, a linked hotspot map and CSV/PNG downloads. We also trained a machine-learning model that estimates the chance of fire in a chosen area over the coming week, clearly labelled as experimental, not an official warning.

Researchers get a clean, downloadable 20+ year dataset instead of two incompatible ones. Farmers, people living near forests, journalists and local authorities get something they can actually read: when the fire season normally starts, whether this year is unusual, and what next week might look like.

We used Python (pandas, DuckDB, FastAPI, scikit-learn) for the data and the model, TypeScript with React, MapLibre and ECharts for the website, and Docker with GitHub Actions for hosting. The only data source is NASA FIRMS.

Instead of one more map of red dots, we show fire as a calendar anyone understands in seconds. We built for both scientists and ordinary people, so the site is honest about what is history, what is a forecast, and how reliable each number is.
